statement: Let $f$ be [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at every point of $[a, b]$ with [continuous](c:continuous-function) [derivative](c:derivative) $f'$, and let $g\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then $\int_a^b g(f(x))\, f'(x)\, dx = \int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} g(u)\, du$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at every point of $[a, b]$, with derivative $f'$.
The [derivative](c:derivative) $f'$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$.
The function $g\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous.

conclusion: $\int_a^b g(f(x))\, f'(x)\, dx = \int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} g(u)\, du$: the [integral](c:integral) does not change under the substitution $u = f(x)$.

formal.difference: The declaration lets $g$ take values in any real normed space and allows either order of $a$ and $b$.

proofs.name: Antiderivative and chain rule
proofs.slogan: Differentiate $x \mapsto \int_{f(a)}^{f(x)} g$ by the chain rule, then integrate that derivative back with the fundamental theorem of calculus.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for either order of $f(a)$ and $f(b)$; for $a = b$ both sides are zero.

roles.why: Differentiability of $f$ lets the chain rule differentiate $G = F \circ f$.
Continuity of $f'$ makes $G'$ continuous, so the second fundamental theorem applies to it.
Continuity of $g$ makes $F(y) = \int_{f(a)}^{y} g$ an [antiderivative](c:antiderivative) of $g$ and keeps $g \circ f$ continuous.

steps.slogan: Define $G(x) = \int_{f(a)}^{f(x)} g(u)\, du$ for $x \in [a, b]$.
steps.detail: Set $F(y) = \int_{f(a)}^{y} g(u)\, du$ and $G = F \circ f$. Then $G(a) = 0$ and $G(b) = \int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} g(u)\, du$, the right side of the formula.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the integral $F$ with respect to its upper limit.
steps.detail: Because $g$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function), the first fundamental theorem of calculus gives $F'(y) = g(y)$ for every $y$. So $F$ is an [antiderivative](c:antiderivative) of $g$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $G = F \circ f$ by the chain rule.
steps.detail: At each $x \in [a, b]$, $f$ has derivative $f'(x)$ and $F$ has derivative $g(f(x))$ at $f(x)$. The chain rule gives $G'(x) = g(f(x))\, f'(x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the integrand $g(f(x))\, f'(x)$ is continuous on $[a, b]$.
steps.detail: The function $f$ is continuous because it is differentiable, so $g \circ f$ is continuous. Its product with the continuous $f'$ is continuous, hence integrable on $[a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Integrate $G'$ over $[a, b]$ with the second fundamental theorem of calculus.
steps.detail: The derivative $G' = (g \circ f)\, f'$ is continuous, so $\int_a^b g(f(x))\, f'(x)\, dx = G(b) - G(a) = \int_{f(a)}^{f(b)} g(u)\, du$.

concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability of $f$ feeds the chain rule for $F \circ f$.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $g$ and $f'$ lets both fundamental theorems apply.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative $f'$ is the factor that the substitution produces.
concepts.c:integral: Both sides are definite integrals, compared through the function $G$.
concepts.c:antiderivative: The function $F$ is an antiderivative of $g$, composed with $f$.

statement: For a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ with [center](c:center) $Z(G)$, $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i=1}^{r} [G : C_G(x_i)]$, where $x_1, \dots, x_r$ represent the [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class) with more than one element and $C_G(x_i)$ is the [centralizer](c:commutant) of $x_i$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).

conclusion: The order of $G$ is the order of its center plus the [indices](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $[G : C_G(x_i)]$ of the centralizers of representatives of the noncentral conjugacy classes.

formal.difference: The declaration sums the sizes of the noncentral conjugacy classes and does not rewrite each size as the index $[G : C_G(x)]$.

proofs.name: Decomposition into conjugacy classes
proofs.slogan: Split the group into conjugacy classes, collect the one-element classes into the center, and count each other class by its stabilizer.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For an abelian group no class has more than one element, and the formula reads $|G| = |Z(G)|$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes every class size and the sum over the classes a finite number.

steps.slogan: Partition $G$ into the [orbits](c:orbit) of the conjugation action.
steps.detail: The [group action](c:group-action) $g \cdot x = g x g^{-1}$ has the [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class) as its orbits. Orbits are disjoint and cover $G$, so $|G|$ is the sum of the class sizes.

steps.slogan: Show that the class of $x$ has one element exactly when $x$ is central.
steps.detail: The class of $x$ is $\{x\}$ if and only if $g x g^{-1} = x$ for every $g$, that is, $x \in Z(G)$. So $x \mapsto \{x\}$ is a bijection from the [center](c:center) onto the one-element classes.

steps.slogan: Split the sum into the one-element classes and the other classes.
steps.detail: By step 2 the one-element classes contribute $|Z(G)|$ to the sum of step 1. The other classes are those of $x_1, \dots, x_r$, so $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_i |\mathrm{Cl}(x_i)|$.

steps.slogan: Count each class through the cosets of the centralizer of its representative.
steps.detail: The stabilizer of $x$ under conjugation is the [centralizer](c:commutant) $C_G(x)$. The map $g\, C_G(x) \mapsto g x g^{-1}$ is a well-defined bijection from the cosets onto the class, so $|\mathrm{Cl}(x)| = [G : C_G(x)]$.

steps.slogan: Replace each class size by its index to get the class equation.
steps.detail: Step 4 turns the formula of step 3 into $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i=1}^{r} [G : C_G(x_i)]$, with each index a divisor of $|G|$.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness of $G$ makes the class sizes and their sum finite.
concepts.c:center: The center collects exactly the one-element conjugacy classes.
concepts.c:conjugacy-class: The classes are the blocks of the partition that the equation counts.
concepts.c:commutant: The centralizer is the stabilizer whose index gives a class size.
concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: Each noncentral class size is the index of a centralizer.
concepts.c:orbit: Conjugacy classes are the orbits of the conjugation action.
concepts.c:group-action: Conjugation is the action whose orbits partition the group.

source.note: mathlib sums the class sizes (sum_conjClasses_card_eq_card), splits off the noncentral classes (Finset.sum_sdiff) and matches the center with the one-element classes (ConjClasses.mk_bijOn); step 4, the index form, is added.

statement: For a subset $s$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space), every proper [filter](c:filter) that contains $s$ has a cluster point in $s$ if and only if every [open cover](c:open-cover) of $s$ has a finite subcover. A cluster point of a filter is a point whose every neighborhood meets every set of the filter.

hypotheses.text: The set $s$ is a subset of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$.

conclusion: The filter definition of a [compact](c:compact-space) set, which mathlib uses, agrees with the open-cover definition.

formal.difference: The declaration only quantifies over covers indexed by types in the universe of $X$; this loses nothing, since a cover can be indexed by its own members.

proofs.name: Finitely covered sets and separating neighborhoods
proofs.slogan: A cover without a finite subcover gives a proper filter with no cluster point in $s$, and a filter with no cluster point gives such a cover.
proofs.scope: Both directions, each by contradiction. The empty set satisfies both conditions: no proper filter contains it, and the empty subcover covers it.

roles.why: The ambient [topological space](c:topological-space) supplies the open sets and neighborhoods of both definitions.

steps.slogan: Form the [filter](c:filter) of sets whose complements finitely many $U_i$ cover.
steps.detail: Let $\{U_i\}$ be an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $s$, and call a set small if finitely many $U_i$ cover it. Small sets are closed under subsets and finite unions, so the complements of small sets form a filter $f$.

steps.slogan: Restrict the filter to $s$ and take a cluster point $x \in s$.
steps.detail: Suppose that $s$ is not small. Then no set of $f$ misses $s$, so $f$ and $s$ generate a proper filter that contains $s$. By the filter condition it has a cluster point $x \in s$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the cluster point with the cover set that contains it.
steps.detail: Some $U_i$ contains $x$. The set $U_i$ is small, so $X \setminus U_i$ is in $f$, and it misses the neighborhood $U_i$ of $x$. This contradicts that $x$ is a cluster point, so finitely many $U_i$ cover $s$.

steps.slogan: Assume a proper filter without cluster points in $s$ and separate each point from it.
steps.detail: Let $f$ be a proper filter that contains $s$ and has no cluster point in $s$. For each $x \in s$ choose an open set $U_x \ni x$ and a set $A_x \in f$ with $U_x \cap A_x = \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Select a finite subcover and intersect the matching filter sets.
steps.detail: The sets $U_x$ form an open cover of $s$, so finitely many $U_{x_1}, \dots, U_{x_n}$ cover $s$. Then $s \cap A_{x_1} \cap \dots \cap A_{x_n}$ is in $f$ but is empty, which contradicts that $f$ is proper.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence of the definitions.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 show that the filter condition gives finite subcovers. Steps 4 and 5 show that finite subcovers give the filter condition, so $s$ is [compact](c:compact-space) in one sense exactly when it is compact in the other.

concepts.c:topological-space: The topology gives the open sets and neighborhoods of both definitions.
concepts.c:filter: Filters give mathlib's definition of compactness through cluster points.
concepts.c:open-cover: Open covers give the classical definition that the theorem matches.
concepts.c:compact-space: The theorem shows that two definitions of compactness agree.

source.note: mathlib proves IsCompact.elim_finite_subcover through IsCompact.induction_on (the filter of complements of finitely covered sets) and isCompact_of_finite_subcover by neighborhoods disjoint from filter sets.

statement: An infinite sequence $X_1, X_2, \dots$ of real [random variables](c:random-variable) is [exchangeable](c:exchangeability) if and only if, for some random probability measure $\mu$, the $X_i$ are [iid](c:iid-random-variables) with law $\mu$ given $\mu$. Then the law of the sequence is the [mixture](c:mixture-of-distributions) $\int \nu^{\otimes \infty}\, \Pi(d\nu)$, where $\Pi$ is the law of $\mu$.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $X_1, X_2, \dots$ is infinite.
The $X_i$ are real [random variables](c:random-variable) on one probability space.

conclusion: Exchangeability is equivalent to [conditional independence](c:conditional-independence) with a common random law, and the law of the sequence is a mixture of iid laws.

proofs.name: Reverse martingale of symmetric averages
proofs.slogan: Symmetric averages over distinct indices form a reverse martingale, and their limits factor into products, which makes the coordinates conditionally iid.
proofs.scope: Both directions; step 1 is the direction from a mixture to exchangeability. Finite exchangeable sequences need not be mixtures, so the proof needs infinitely many terms.

roles.why: Infinitely many coordinates let the averages run over all $n \to \infty$.
Real values give a regular conditional law $\mu$ of $X_1$, and a product $\sigma$-algebra for the mixture.

steps.slogan: Check that every mixture of iid laws is exchangeable.
steps.detail: A product law $\nu^{\otimes\infty}$ does not change when finitely many coordinates are permuted. Integration over $\nu$ keeps this invariance, so a [mixture](c:mixture-of-distributions) of such laws is [exchangeable](c:exchangeability).

steps.slogan: Write [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation) given $\mathcal{E}_n$ as averages over distinct indices.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{E}_n$ hold the events of the sequence that are invariant under permutations of the first $n$ indices; they decrease to $\mathcal{E} = \bigcap_n \mathcal{E}_n$. For bounded $\varphi$ of $k \le n$ variables, exchangeability gives $\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_1, \dots, X_k) \mid \mathcal{E}_n] = A_n(\varphi)$, the mean of $\varphi(X_{i_1}, \dots, X_{i_k})$ over distinct $i_1, \dots, i_k \le n$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit by reverse [martingale](c:martingale) convergence.
steps.detail: The averages $A_n(\varphi) = \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_1, \dots, X_k) \mid \mathcal{E}_n]$ form a reverse martingale for the decreasing $\mathcal{E}_n$. So $A_n(\varphi) \to \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_1, \dots, X_k) \mid \mathcal{E}]$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Compare the average of a product with the product of the averages.
steps.detail: For $\varphi = f(x_1, \dots, x_{k-1})\, g(x_k)$, the product $A_n(f)\, A_n(g)$ is $A_n(\varphi)$ plus terms with a repeated index of total weight $O(1/n)$. In the limit, $\mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \dots, X_{k-1})\, g(X_k) \mid \mathcal{E}] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, \dots, X_{k-1}) \mid \mathcal{E}]\; \mathbb{E}[g(X_1) \mid \mathcal{E}]$.

steps.slogan: Iterate the factorization to make the coordinates conditionally iid.
steps.detail: Induction on $k$ gives $\mathbb{E}[\prod_{j \le k} f_j(X_j) \mid \mathcal{E}] = \prod_{j \le k} \mu(f_j)$, where $\mu$ is a regular conditional law of $X_1$ given $\mathcal{E}$. So, given $\mu$, the $X_i$ are [conditionally independent](c:conditional-independence) with common law $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the conditional product law to get the mixture.
steps.detail: Expectations give $P(X \in C) = \mathbb{E}[\mu^{\otimes\infty}(C)] = \int \nu^{\otimes\infty}(C)\, \Pi(d\nu)$ for cylinder sets $C$. Cylinders form a $\pi$-system that generates the product $\sigma$-algebra, so the identity holds for all $C$; with step 1 this gives the equivalence.

concepts.c:random-variable: The theorem is about a sequence of real random variables.
concepts.c:exchangeability: Exchangeability makes the conditional expectations symmetric averages.
concepts.c:iid-random-variables: The conclusion says the coordinates are iid given $\mu$.
concepts.c:mixture-of-distributions: The law of the sequence is an average of iid laws.
concepts.c:conditional-independence: The factorization of step 4 is conditional independence given $\mathcal{E}$.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: Conditional expectations given $\mathcal{E}_n$ are the symmetric averages.
concepts.c:martingale: Reverse martingale convergence gives the limits of the averages.

source.note: The reverse-martingale proof, as in R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, the section on backwards martingales (de Finetti's theorem).

statement: Let $E$, $F$, $G$ be [normed spaces](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If $f\colon E \to F$ has [Fréchet derivative](c:frechet-derivative) $f'$ at $x$ and $g\colon F \to G$ has Fréchet derivative $g'$ at $f(x)$, then $g \circ f$ has Fréchet derivative $g' \circ f'$ at $x$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon E \to F$ has [Fréchet derivative](c:frechet-derivative) $f'$ at $x$, a continuous [linear map](c:linear-map).
The map $g\colon F \to G$ has Fréchet derivative $g'$ at $f(x)$.

conclusion: The [composition](c:composition) $g \circ f$ has [derivative](c:derivative) $g' \circ f'$ at $x$; in one variable, $(g \circ f)'(x) = g'(f(x))\, f'(x)$.

formal.difference: The declaration works over any nontrivially normed field, not only $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.

proofs.name: Composition of remainders
proofs.slogan: Substitute the expansion of $f$ into the expansion of $g$ and show that both remainders are small compared with $\|h\|$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof never divides by $f(x + h) - f(x)$, so it also covers maps $f$ that are constant near $x$.

roles.why: The expansion of $f$ gives a remainder $r(h) = o(\|h\|)$ and a linear bound on $f(x + h) - f(x)$.
The expansion of $g$ at $f(x)$ gives a remainder $s(k) = o(\|k\|)$.

steps.slogan: Write the first-order expansion of $f$ at $x$ with a small remainder.
steps.detail: We have $f(x + h) = f(x) + f'h + r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\| / \|h\| \to 0$. So $k(h) = f(x + h) - f(x)$ satisfies $\|k(h)\| \le (\|f'\| + 1)\|h\|$ for small $h$, and $k(h) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Write the first-order expansion of $g$ at the point $f(x)$.
steps.detail: We have $g(f(x) + k) = g(f(x)) + g'k + s(k)$, where $s(0) = 0$ and $\|s(k)\| / \|k\| \to 0$ as $k \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the increment $k(h)$ of $f$ into the expansion of $g$.
steps.detail: With $k = k(h) = f'h + r(h)$, the expansion of $g$ gives $g(f(x + h)) - g(f(x)) - g'f'h = g'(r(h)) + s(k(h))$.

steps.slogan: Bound the first remainder by the [operator norm](c:operator-norm) of $g'$.
steps.detail: Because $g'$ is a continuous [linear map](c:linear-map), $\|g'(r(h))\| \le \|g'\|\, \|r(h)\|$. This is $o(\|h\|)$ because $r(h)$ is.

steps.slogan: Bound the second remainder through the linear bound on $k(h)$.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, $\|s(k)\| \le \varepsilon \|k\|$ for small $k$. Since $k(h) \to 0$ and $\|k(h)\| \le (\|f'\| + 1)\|h\|$, we get $\|s(k(h))\| \le \varepsilon (\|f'\| + 1)\|h\|$ for small $h$.

steps.slogan: Add the two bounds to get the derivative $g' \circ f'$.
steps.detail: The remainder of $g \circ f$ with respect to the continuous linear map $g' \circ f'$ is $o(\|h\|)$. This is the definition of the Fréchet derivative, so $(g \circ f)'(x) = g' \circ f'$.

concepts.c:normed-space: Norms measure the size of the increments and the remainders.
concepts.c:frechet-derivative: Both hypotheses and the conclusion are Fréchet derivatives.
concepts.c:linear-map: A bounded linear map turns a small remainder into a small remainder.
concepts.c:composition: The theorem computes the derivative of a composition.
concepts.c:derivative: In one variable the result is the familiar chain rule.
concepts.c:operator-norm: The operator norm bounds $g'$ applied to the remainder.

source.note: mathlib applies HasFDerivAtFilter.comp, which composes the little-o remainders, with the continuity of $f$ at $x$ (HasFDerivAt.continuousAt).

statement: Any two [bases](c:basis-of-a-vector-space) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a [field](c:field) have the same [cardinality](c:cardinal-number), finite or infinite.

hypotheses.text: The space $V$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a [field](c:field) $K$.
The sets $B$ and $C$ are [bases](c:basis-of-a-vector-space) of $V$.

conclusion: $|B| = |C|$, so the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) of $V$ is well defined.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for modules over any ring with invariant basis number, which includes all fields, and compares the cardinalities through universe lifts.

proofs.name: Exchange for finite bases, supports for infinite bases
proofs.slogan: Compare finite bases by the exchange lemma, and bound an infinite basis by the finite supports of the elements of the other basis.
proofs.scope: Case split: some basis is finite, or both bases are infinite. The zero space has only the empty basis, which the finite case covers.

roles.why: Over a field the exchange lemma holds, which settles the finite case.
Coordinates in $B$ give the supports, and the maximal independence of $C$ makes them cover $B$.

steps.slogan: Show that a finite basis forces the other basis to be finite of the same size.
steps.detail: Let $B$ have $n$ elements. By the exchange lemma every [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) set in $V$ has at most $n$ elements, so $C$ is finite with $m \le n$ elements. The lemma with the roles swapped gives $n \le m$.

steps.slogan: Attach to each $c \in C$ the finite support of its coordinates in $B$.
steps.detail: Each $c \in C$ is a finite [linear combination](c:linear-combination) of elements of $B$. Let $S_c \subseteq B$ be the finite set of basis vectors with a nonzero coefficient in it.

steps.slogan: Show that the supports $S_c$ together cover the whole basis $B$.
steps.detail: Suppose that $b \in B$ lies in no $S_c$. Every combination of elements of $C$ has $b$-coefficient zero, so $C \cup \{b\}$ is still linearly independent and $b \notin C$. This contradicts that the basis $C$ is a maximal independent set.

steps.slogan: Bound $|B|$ by $|C|$ when the basis $B$ is infinite.
steps.detail: An infinite set covered by finite sets $S_c$, $c \in C$, has cardinality at most $\aleph_0 \cdot |C|$. Step 1 excludes a finite $C$, so $C$ is infinite and $\aleph_0 \cdot |C| = |C|$, which gives $|B| \le |C|$.

steps.slogan: Swap the roles of the two bases and compare the two bounds.
steps.detail: If one basis is finite, step 1 gives $|B| = |C|$. Otherwise steps 2 to 4 with $B$ and $C$ swapped give $|C| \le |B|$, and the Cantor-Bernstein theorem gives $|B| = |C|$.

concepts.c:basis-of-a-vector-space: The theorem compares the sizes of two bases.
concepts.c:vector-space: The space whose bases the theorem compares.
concepts.c:field: Over a field the exchange lemma settles the finite case.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: Sizes of infinite bases are compared as cardinal numbers.
concepts.c:dimension-of-a-vector-space: The common size of the bases defines the dimension.
concepts.c:linear-independence: Independence bounds the size of a set by a spanning set.
concepts.c:linear-combination: Coordinates in $B$ give the finite supports $S_c$.

statement: Let $V\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous and bounded below. Let $u$ be bounded and continuous on $[0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d$, of class $C^{1,2}$ on $(0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d$, and solve the [heat equation](c:heat-equation) with potential $\partial_t u = \tfrac12 \Delta u - V u$, with $u(0, \cdot) = f$. Then $u(t, x) = \mathbb{E}_x\big[e^{-\int_0^t V(B_s)\, ds} f(B_t)\big]$ for a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ from $x$.

hypotheses.text: The potential $V\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous and bounded below by $-c$.
The function $u$ is bounded and continuous on $[0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d$ and of class $C^{1,2}$ on $(0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d$.
The function $u$ solves the [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation) $\partial_t u = \tfrac12 \Delta u - V u$ on $(0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d$ with $u(0, \cdot) = f$.

conclusion: For $0 \le t \le T$, $u(t, x)$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value) of $e^{-\int_0^t V(B_s)\, ds} f(B_t)$, a [path integral](c:path-integral) over Brownian paths from $x$.

proofs.name: Martingale from Itô's formula
proofs.slogan: Follow the solution backward in time along a Brownian path with the weight $e^{-\int V}$, show that this is a martingale, and compare its expectations at both ends.
proofs.scope: The case $0 < t \le T$; for $t = 0$ both sides equal $f(x)$. The argument also shows that a bounded solution is unique.

roles.why: The bound $V \ge -c$ makes the weight at most $e^{ct}$, so the process stays bounded.
Smoothness allows Itô's formula, and boundedness and continuity control the process and its limit.
The equation cancels the drift in Itô's formula, and the initial value gives $f(B_t)$ at the end.

steps.slogan: Define the weighted process $M_s = Z_s\, u(t - s, B_s)$ for $0 \le s < t$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) started at $x$ and $Z_s = e^{-\int_0^s V(B_r)\, dr}$. Then $M_0 = u(t, x)$, the left side of the formula.

steps.slogan: Expand $M$ by Itô's formula and cancel the drift with the equation.
steps.detail: On $[0, t - \varepsilon]$, Itô's formula gives $dM_s = Z_s\, (-\partial_t u + \tfrac12 \Delta u - V u)(t - s, B_s)\, ds + Z_s\, \nabla u(t - s, B_s) \cdot dB_s$. The equation makes the $ds$ term zero, so $M$ is an [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) and a local martingale.

steps.slogan: Show that the bounded local martingale $M$ is a true [martingale](c:martingale).
steps.detail: Because $V \ge -c$ and $u$ is bounded, $|M_s| \le e^{ct} \sup |u|$ on $[0, t - \varepsilon]$. A bounded local martingale is a martingale, so $\mathbb{E}[M_{t - \varepsilon}] = M_0 = u(t, x)$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon \to 0$ with the dominated convergence theorem.
steps.detail: Continuity of $u$ and of the Brownian path gives $M_{t - \varepsilon} \to Z_t\, u(0, B_t) = Z_t f(B_t)$ almost surely. The bound $e^{ct} \sup|u|$ allows dominated convergence, so $u(t, x) = \mathbb{E}_x[Z_t f(B_t)]$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) in the formula.

concepts.c:heat-equation: The equation is the heat equation with an added potential term.
concepts.c:brownian-motion: The expectation runs over the paths of Brownian motion.
concepts.c:partial-differential-equation: The formula represents the solution of this equation.
concepts.c:expected-value: The formula writes the solution as an expected value.
concepts.c:path-integral: The expectation is a Wiener path integral over Brownian paths.
concepts.c:ito-integral: Itô's formula writes $M$ as a stochastic integral without drift.
concepts.c:martingale: The martingale property gives equal expectations at both ends.

source.note: The standard Itô-formula proof, as in I. Karatzas and S. E. Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus, section 4.4 (the formulas of Feynman and Kac).

statement: A [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n$ elements has exactly $\binom{n}{k}$ [subsets](c:subset) with $k$ elements, where the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) is $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$ for $k \le n$ and $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$.

hypotheses.text: The set $S$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n$ elements.
The number $k$ is a natural number.

conclusion: The number of $k$-element subsets of $S$ is $\binom{n}{k}$, given by the [factorial](c:factorial) formula.

formal.difference: The declaration identifies the count with Nat.choose, which mathlib defines by Pascal's rule. The factorial formula is the separate declaration Nat.choose_eq_factorial_div_factorial.

proofs.name: Induction with Pascal's rule
proofs.slogan: Split the subsets by whether they contain a fixed element, which gives Pascal's rule and an induction on $n$.
proofs.scope: Induction on $n$ for all $k$ at once, then a check that the factorial formula solves the same recursion. The cases $n = 0$ and $k = 0$ are the base cases.

roles.why: Finiteness allows induction on the number $n$ of elements.
The recursion lowers $k$ by one, so the claim is proved for all natural $k$ together.

steps.slogan: Check the counts for the empty set and for $k = 0$.
steps.detail: The empty set has one subset with $0$ elements and none with more, which matches $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k+1} = 0$. Every set has exactly one $0$-element subset, which matches $\binom{n}{0} = 1$.

steps.slogan: Split the $(k+1)$-subsets of $T \cup \{a\}$ by whether they contain $a$.
steps.detail: Let $a \notin T$ and $|T| = n$. A $(k+1)$-subset of $T \cup \{a\}$ without $a$ is a $(k+1)$-subset of $T$. One with $a$ is $\{a\} \cup R$ for a unique $k$-subset $R$ of $T$.

steps.slogan: Add the two counts with Pascal's rule and close the induction.
steps.detail: By induction the two kinds number $\binom{n}{k+1}$ and $\binom{n}{k}$, and Pascal's rule gives $\binom{n}{k+1} + \binom{n}{k} = \binom{n+1}{k+1}$. So the count is the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) of Pascal's recursion.

steps.slogan: Check that the [factorial](c:factorial) formula satisfies the same recursion and initial values.
steps.detail: For $k < n$, $\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} + \frac{n!}{(k+1)!\,(n-k-1)!} = \frac{(n+1)!}{(k+1)!\,(n-k)!}$, and the values for $k = n$ and $k > n$ match $1$ and $0$. A recursion with given initial values has one solution, so $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$.

concepts.c:finite-set: Induction runs over the size of the finite set.
concepts.c:subset: The theorem counts the subsets of a given size.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The count is the binomial coefficient defined by Pascal's rule.
concepts.c:factorial: The closed formula expresses the count by factorials.

source.note: mathlib reduces to lists (List.length_sublistsLen): sublistsLen_succ_cons splits by the first element and Nat.choose_succ_succ is Pascal's rule; the factorial check is Nat.choose_eq_factorial_div_factorial.

proofs.name: Counting ordered selections twice
proofs.slogan: Count the ordered lists of $k$ distinct elements directly and through the subsets that they come from.
proofs.scope: The case $k \le n$. For $k > n$ no subset has $k$ elements, so the count is $0$.

roles.why: The size $n$ gives $n$ choices for the first entry, $n - 1$ for the next, and so on.
The size $k$ fixes the length of the lists and the $k!$ orderings of each subset.

steps.slogan: Count the ordered lists of $k$ distinct elements of $S$.
steps.detail: There are $n$ choices for the first entry, $n - 1$ for the second, and $n - k + 1$ for the last. So there are $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1) = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$ such lists.

steps.slogan: Group the lists by the set of their entries.
steps.detail: The entries of each list form a $k$-element [subset](c:subset) of $S$. Each such subset is the set of entries of exactly $k!$ lists, its orderings as [permutations](c:permutation).

steps.slogan: Equate the two counts and divide by $k!$.
steps.detail: If $N$ is the number of $k$-subsets, then $N \cdot k! = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$. Hence $N = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} = \binom{n}{k}$.

concepts.c:finite-set: The finite size gives the number of choices for each entry.
concepts.c:subset: The lists fall into classes, one for each subset.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The binomial coefficient is the quotient that the double count gives.
concepts.c:factorial: Factorials count the lists and the orderings of a subset.
concepts.c:permutation: Each subset has $k!$ orderings, its permutations.

source.note: The classical double-counting proof of the formula for binomial coefficients.

statement: For a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $\varphi\colon G \to H$ with [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) $K = \ker \varphi$, the subgroup $K$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$, and $gK \mapsto \varphi(g)$ is a well-defined [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) from the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/K$ onto the [image](c:image) $\varphi(G)$.

hypotheses.text: The map $\varphi\colon G \to H$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism).

formal.difference: The declaration constructs the isomorphism $g \ker\varphi \mapsto \varphi(g)$ as data; normality of the kernel is the separate instance MonoidHom.normal_ker.

proofs.name: Induced map on cosets
proofs.slogan: Let $\varphi$ act on the cosets of its kernel, and check that this induced map is a well-defined bijective homomorphism onto the image.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. When $\varphi$ is injective the kernel is trivial and the theorem gives $G \cong \varphi(G)$.

roles.why: The homomorphism property makes the kernel normal, the induced map well defined and multiplicative.

steps.slogan: Show that the kernel is a normal subgroup of $G$.
steps.detail: The kernel is a subgroup because $\varphi$ keeps products and inverses. For $k \in K$ and $g \in G$, $\varphi(g k g^{-1}) = \varphi(g)\, \varphi(k)\, \varphi(g)^{-1} = 1$, so $K$ is normal and the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/K$ exists.

steps.slogan: Define $\bar\varphi(gK) = \varphi(g)$ and check that it does not depend on $g$.
steps.detail: If $gK = g'K$, then $g^{-1} g' \in K$, so $\varphi(g') = \varphi(g)\, \varphi(g^{-1} g') = \varphi(g)$. So $\bar\varphi\colon G/K \to \varphi(G)$ is well defined.

steps.slogan: Check that the induced map $\bar\varphi$ keeps products.
steps.detail: The product of cosets is $gK \cdot g'K = gg'K$, so $\bar\varphi(gK \cdot g'K) = \varphi(g g') = \varphi(g)\, \varphi(g') = \bar\varphi(gK)\, \bar\varphi(g'K)$ because $\varphi$ is a homomorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that only the coset $K$ maps to the identity.
steps.detail: If $\bar\varphi(gK) = 1$, then $\varphi(g) = 1$, so $g \in K$ and $gK = K$. A homomorphism with trivial kernel is injective, so $\bar\varphi$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Show that every element of the image is a value of $\bar\varphi$.
steps.detail: Each element of $\varphi(G)$ has the form $\varphi(g) = \bar\varphi(gK)$ for some $g \in G$, so $\bar\varphi$ maps onto the [image](c:image).

steps.slogan: Conclude that the bijective homomorphism $\bar\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: The inverse map of a bijective homomorphism is again a homomorphism. So $\bar\varphi$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) $G/K \cong \varphi(G)$.

concepts.c:group-homomorphism: The theorem studies a homomorphism through its kernel and image.
concepts.c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism: The kernel is the subgroup that the quotient removes.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of the kernel makes the cosets a group.
concepts.c:isomorphism: The induced map is the isomorphism of the conclusion.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The quotient $G/K$ is the domain of the induced map.
concepts.c:image: The image $\varphi(G)$ is the target of the isomorphism.

source.note: mathlib builds MulEquiv.ofBijective from rangeKerLift (the map $gK \mapsto \varphi(g)$, through QuotientGroup.lift) with rangeKerLift_injective and rangeKerLift_surjective.

statement: If $\varphi\colon U \to \mathbb{R}$ is [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\gamma\colon [a, b] \to U$ is a piecewise $C^1$ [curve](c:curve), then the [line integral](c:line-integral) of the [gradient](c:gradient) is $\int_\gamma \nabla \varphi \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \varphi(\gamma(b)) - \varphi(\gamma(a))$.

hypotheses.text: The function $\varphi$ is [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.
The [curve](c:curve) $\gamma\colon [a, b] \to U$ is piecewise $C^1$.

conclusion: The line integral of $\nabla\varphi$ along $\gamma$ equals $\varphi(\gamma(b)) - \varphi(\gamma(a))$, so it depends only on the end points.

proofs.name: Chain rule and fundamental theorem on each piece
proofs.slogan: On each smooth piece the integrand is the derivative of $\varphi \circ \gamma$, so the fundamental theorem of calculus evaluates it and the pieces telescope.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For a closed curve the value is $0$.

roles.why: Continuous differentiability gives the chain rule and a continuous integrand.
The curve splits into finitely many $C^1$ pieces with continuous velocity.

steps.slogan: Split $[a, b]$ at the corners of $\gamma$ into $C^1$ pieces.
steps.detail: Choose $a = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_m = b$ such that $\gamma$ is $C^1$ on each $[t_{k-1}, t_k]$. By definition, the [line integral](c:line-integral) is the sum of the integrals $\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} \nabla\varphi(\gamma(t)) \cdot \gamma'(t)\, dt$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $\varphi \circ \gamma$ on each piece by the chain rule.
steps.detail: On $[t_{k-1}, t_k]$ the chain rule gives $(\varphi \circ \gamma)'(t) = \nabla\varphi(\gamma(t)) \cdot \gamma'(t)$. This derivative is continuous because $\nabla\varphi$ and $\gamma'$ are continuous.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the integral over each piece with the fundamental theorem of calculus.
steps.detail: On $[t_{k-1}, t_k]$ the integrand is the continuous derivative of $\varphi \circ \gamma$. So its integral is $\varphi(\gamma(t_k)) - \varphi(\gamma(t_{k-1}))$.

steps.slogan: Sum over the pieces and cancel the interior end values.
steps.detail: The sum $\sum_{k=1}^{m} [\varphi(\gamma(t_k)) - \varphi(\gamma(t_{k-1}))]$ telescopes to $\varphi(\gamma(b)) - \varphi(\gamma(a))$. This is the line integral of the [gradient](c:gradient) along $\gamma$.

concepts.c:continuously-differentiable-map: Continuous differentiability gives the chain rule and a continuous integrand.
concepts.c:curve: The integral runs along this piecewise smooth curve.
concepts.c:line-integral: The line integral is the sum of the integrals over the pieces.
concepts.c:gradient: The integrand is the gradient field of $\varphi$.

source.note: The standard proof by the chain rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus, as in J. Stewart, Calculus, the section on the fundamental theorem for line integrals.

statement: For every natural number $n$, the number of [partitions](c:integer-partition) of $n$ into odd parts equals the number of partitions of $n$ into distinct parts.

hypotheses.text: The number $n$ is a natural number, $n \ge 0$.

conclusion: The partitions of $n$ into odd parts and the partitions of $n$ into distinct parts are equal in number.

proofs.name: Equal generating functions
proofs.slogan: Write both counts as coefficients of infinite products and turn one product into the other with $1 + x^k = (1 - x^{2k})/(1 - x^k)$.
proofs.scope: All $n$ at once, as an identity of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) over $\mathbb{Z}$. The case $n = 0$ is the empty partition on both sides.

roles.why: The count for $n$ is the coefficient of $x^n$ in each series.

steps.slogan: Write the [generating function](c:generating-function) of partitions into odd parts as a product.
steps.detail: A choice of multiplicity for each odd part $k$ gives $\sum_n o(n)\, x^n = \prod_{k \text{ odd}} (1 + x^k + x^{2k} + \cdots) = \prod_{k \text{ odd}} \frac{1}{1 - x^k}$. Each coefficient depends on finitely many factors, so the product is defined.

steps.slogan: Write the generating function of partitions into distinct parts as a product.
steps.detail: In a partition into distinct parts each part $k \ge 1$ occurs at most once. So $\sum_n d(n)\, x^n = \prod_{k \ge 1} (1 + x^k)$.

steps.slogan: Multiply both products by the series $P = \prod_{k \ge 1} (1 - x^k)$.
steps.detail: The odd factors cancel: $P \prod_{k \text{ odd}} \frac{1}{1 - x^k} = \prod_{k \text{ even}} (1 - x^k) = \prod_{j \ge 1} (1 - x^{2j})$. Also $P \prod_{k \ge 1} (1 + x^k) = \prod_{k \ge 1} (1 - x^{2k})$, the same product.

steps.slogan: Cancel the nonzero series $P$ in the integral domain of formal power series.
steps.detail: The series $P$ has constant term $1$, so it is not zero, and $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$ has no zero divisors. Hence the two generating functions are equal.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $x^n$ in the two equal series.
steps.detail: Equal [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) have equal coefficients. So $o(n) = d(n)$ for every $n \ge 0$.

concepts.c:integer-partition: The theorem compares two classes of partitions of $n$.
concepts.c:generating-function: Generating functions turn the two counts into infinite products.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: The product identities hold in the ring of formal power series.

source.note: mathlib specializes Glaisher's theorem (card_restricted_eq_card_countRestricted, $m = 2$), proved by generating functions: both products times $\prod (1 - X^{i+1})$ become $\prod (1 - X^{(i+1)m})$, then mul_right_cancel₀.

proofs.name: Binary splitting and merging
proofs.slogan: Split each distinct part $2^a m$ with $m$ odd into $2^a$ copies of $m$, and undo this by merging copies along binary expansions.
proofs.scope: A bijection for each $n$. The empty partition of $0$ corresponds to itself.

roles.why: Both maps keep the sum $n$ of the parts.

steps.slogan: Split each distinct part $2^a m$, with $m$ odd, into $2^a$ parts equal to $m$.
steps.detail: Every positive integer is $2^a m$ with $m$ odd in exactly one way. Splitting each part keeps the sum $n$ and gives a [partition](c:integer-partition) into odd parts.

steps.slogan: Merge the copies of each odd part along the [binary](c:binary-digit) expansion of its multiplicity.
steps.detail: If the odd part $m$ occurs $r$ times, write $r = 2^{a_1} + \dots + 2^{a_j}$ with distinct exponents. Replace the $r$ copies by the parts $2^{a_1} m, \dots, 2^{a_j} m$, which keeps the sum $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the merged parts are pairwise distinct.
steps.detail: Two merged parts $2^{a} m$ and $2^{a'} m'$ are equal only if $m = m'$ and $a = a'$, by uniqueness of the odd part and the power of $2$. The exponents for one $m$ are distinct, so all merged parts are distinct.

steps.slogan: Check that splitting and merging undo each other.
steps.detail: In a partition into distinct parts, the parts with odd part $m$ are $2^{a_1} m, \dots, 2^{a_j} m$ with distinct $a_i$; splitting gives $r = \sum 2^{a_i}$ copies, and the binary expansion of $r$ returns the same $a_i$. Conversely splitting the merged parts returns $r$ copies, so the maps are inverse bijections.

concepts.c:integer-partition: The bijection matches distinct-part partitions with odd-part partitions.
concepts.c:binary-digit: Binary digits of a multiplicity tell how to merge the copies.

source.note: Glaisher's bijection, the standard bijective proof of Euler's partition theorem.

statement: If $u$ and $v$ are [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at every point of $[a, b]$ and their [derivatives](c:derivative) $u'$ and $v'$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[a, b]$, then $\int_a^b u\, v'\, dx = u(b)\, v(b) - u(a)\, v(a) - \int_a^b u'\, v\, dx$.

hypotheses.text: The function $u$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at every point of $[a, b]$, with derivative $u'$.
The function $v$ is differentiable at every point of $[a, b]$, with derivative $v'$.
The [derivatives](c:derivative) $u'$ and $v'$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[a, b]$.

conclusion: $\int_a^b u\, v'\, dx = u(b)\, v(b) - u(a)\, v(a) - \int_a^b u'\, v\, dx$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in any complete normed real algebra, where the order of the factors matters, and either order of $a$ and $b$.

proofs.name: Product rule and fundamental theorem
proofs.slogan: Integrate the product rule $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$ with the fundamental theorem of calculus and move one term to the other side.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For $a = b$ both sides are zero.

roles.why: Differentiability of $u$ gives the product rule and makes $u$ continuous.
Differentiability of $v$ gives the product rule and makes $v$ continuous.
Integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ makes $u'v$, $uv'$ and their sum integrable.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the product $uv$ by the product rule.
steps.detail: At each $x \in [a, b]$, $(uv)'(x) = u'(x)\, v(x) + u(x)\, v'(x)$. This follows from $u(y)v(y) - u(x)v(x) = (u(y) - u(x))\, v(y) + u(x)\, (v(y) - v(x))$ and the continuity of $v$ at $x$.

steps.slogan: Note that $u$ and $v$ are continuous and bounded on $[a, b]$.
steps.detail: A function that is differentiable at a point is [continuous](c:continuous-function) there. A continuous function on the compact interval $[a, b]$ is bounded.

steps.slogan: Show that $u'v$ and $uv'$ are integrable on $[a, b]$.
steps.detail: An integrable function times a bounded continuous function is integrable. So $u'v$, $uv'$ and their sum $(uv)'$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $[a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Integrate $(uv)'$ over $[a, b]$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus.
steps.detail: The product $uv$ is differentiable at every point of $[a, b]$ with integrable derivative. So $\int_a^b (u'v + uv')\, dx = u(b)\,v(b) - u(a)\,v(a)$.

steps.slogan: Split the integral and move $\int_a^b u'v\, dx$ to the other side.
steps.detail: Both $u'v$ and $uv'$ are integrable, so linearity of the integral gives $\int_a^b u v'\, dx = u(b)\,v(b) - u(a)\,v(a) - \int_a^b u' v\, dx$.

concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability gives the product rule at every point.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative of $uv$ is the integrand that the fundamental theorem evaluates.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability lets the fundamental theorem and linearity apply.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $u$ and $v$ makes the products integrable.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with integral_deriv_mul_eq_sub_of_hasDeriv_right (the fundamental theorem for $uv$) and integral_sub, with integrability from IntervalIntegrable.mul_continuousOn.

statement: If a piecewise $C^1$ [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve) in the plane has length ([perimeter](c:perimeter)) $L$ and encloses a region of [area](c:area) $A$, then $L^2 \ge 4\pi A$, with equality if and only if the curve is a circle.

hypotheses.text: The curve is a piecewise $C^1$ [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve) in the plane with length $L$.
The number $A$ is the [area](c:area) of the bounded region inside the curve.

conclusion: $L^2 \ge 4\pi A$, and $L^2 = 4\pi A$ holds only for a circle.

proofs.name: Hurwitz's Fourier series proof
proofs.slogan: Parametrize by arc length, expand the curve in a Fourier series, and compare the Parseval sums for the length and the area.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for piecewise $C^1$ curves, including the equality case. The curve is taken with positive orientation.

roles.why: A piecewise $C^1$ curve has a constant-speed parametrization with square-integrable velocity, so Parseval applies.
Green's theorem writes the enclosed area as an integral over the curve.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the curve by a multiple of arc length on $[0, 2\pi]$.
steps.detail: Write the curve as $z(t) = x(t) + i y(t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, positively oriented, with constant speed $|z'(t)| = L / 2\pi$. Then $\int_0^{2\pi} |z'(t)|^2\, dt = L^2 / 2\pi$.

steps.slogan: Write the enclosed area as a boundary integral by Green's theorem.
steps.detail: Green's theorem gives $A = \frac12 \int_0^{2\pi} (x y' - y x')\, dt = \frac12 \int_0^{2\pi} \operatorname{Im}(\bar z z')\, dt$ for the positively oriented curve.

steps.slogan: Expand $z$ and $z'$ in [Fourier series](c:fourier-series).
steps.detail: Write $z(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c_n e^{int}$. Because $z$ is continuous, periodic and piecewise $C^1$, the Fourier coefficients of $z'$ are $i n c_n$.

steps.slogan: Compute the length and the area with Parseval's identity.
steps.detail: Parseval's identity gives $L^2 / 2\pi = \int_0^{2\pi} |z'|^2\, dt = 2\pi \sum n^2 |c_n|^2$ and $A = \frac12 \operatorname{Im} \int_0^{2\pi} \bar z z'\, dt = \pi \sum n |c_n|^2$. So $L^2 - 4\pi A = 4\pi^2 \sum_{n} (n^2 - n)\, |c_n|^2$.

steps.slogan: Read the inequality and the equality case from the coefficient sum.
steps.detail: Every integer has $n^2 - n = n(n-1) \ge 0$, so $L^2 \ge 4\pi A$. Equality forces $c_n = 0$ for $n \ne 0, 1$, so $z(t) = c_0 + c_1 e^{it}$ is a circle; a circle gives equality.

concepts.c:jordan-curve: A simple closed curve bounds the region whose area is compared.
concepts.c:perimeter: The length of the curve is the perimeter of the region.
concepts.c:area: The area is the quantity that the squared length bounds.
concepts.c:fourier-series: Fourier coefficients turn the length and the area into sums.

source.note: Hurwitz's proof (1902), as in E. M. Stein and R. Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis: An Introduction, chapter 4.

statement: For vectors $u, v, w \in R^3$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the [cross product](c:cross-product) satisfies $u \times (v \times w) + v \times (w \times u) + w \times (u \times v) = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The scalars form a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, and $u, v, w \in R^3$.

conclusion: The cyclic sum of the double cross products is the zero vector.

proofs.name: Leibniz form and antisymmetry
proofs.slogan: Check the Leibniz form of the identity coordinate by coordinate, then turn it into the cyclic form with antisymmetry.
proofs.scope: The whole identity over any commutative ring.

roles.why: Commutativity of $R$ lets the coordinate polynomials cancel.

steps.slogan: Show from the coordinate formula that the cross product is antisymmetric.
steps.detail: With $u \times v = (u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2,\ u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3,\ u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1)$, commutativity of $R$ gives $u \times u = 0$ and $v \times u = -(u \times v)$.

steps.slogan: Check the Leibniz form of the identity coordinate by coordinate.
steps.detail: The Leibniz form is $u \times (v \times w) = (u \times v) \times w + v \times (u \times w)$, and each coordinate of both sides is a cubic polynomial in the coordinates. Expansion in the [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ shows that they agree; so $u \times -$ acts as a derivation of the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) $\times$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite two terms of the Leibniz form with antisymmetry to get the cyclic sum.
steps.detail: Antisymmetry gives $(u \times v) \times w = -\,w \times (u \times v)$ and $v \times (u \times w) = -\,v \times (w \times u)$. Substitution into the Leibniz form gives $u \times (v \times w) + v \times (w \times u) + w \times (u \times v) = 0$.

concepts.c:commutative-ring: Commutativity of the scalars makes the coordinate polynomials cancel.
concepts.c:cross-product: The identity is about cross products of three vectors.
concepts.c:lie-bracket: The Leibniz form says that the cross product acts as a Lie bracket.

source.note: mathlib proves jacobi_cross as lie_jacobi for the Lie ring structure Cross.lieRing on Fin 3 → R, whose Leibniz axiom is leibniz_cross (coordinates and ring) and whose antisymmetry is cross_anticomm.

proofs.name: Triple product expansion
proofs.slogan: Expand each double cross product by the rule $u \times (v \times w) = (u \cdot w)\, v - (u \cdot v)\, w$ and cancel the six terms in pairs.
proofs.scope: The whole identity over any commutative ring.

roles.why: Commutativity proves the expansion rule and makes the dot product symmetric, which pairs the terms.

steps.slogan: Prove the expansion $u \times (v \times w) = (u \cdot w)\, v - (u \cdot v)\, w$ by coordinates.
steps.detail: The first coordinate of the left side is $u_2 (v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1) - u_3 (v_3 w_1 - v_1 w_3)$. Adding and subtracting $u_1 v_1 w_1$ gives $(u \cdot w)\, v_1 - (u \cdot v)\, w_1$; the other coordinates follow by cyclic symmetry.

steps.slogan: Write the expansions of the three cyclic terms.
steps.detail: The rule gives $u \times (v \times w) = (u \cdot w)\, v - (u \cdot v)\, w$, $v \times (w \times u) = (v \cdot u)\, w - (v \cdot w)\, u$ and $w \times (u \times v) = (w \cdot v)\, u - (w \cdot u)\, v$.

steps.slogan: Add the three expansions and cancel the terms in pairs.
steps.detail: Over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) the dot product is symmetric. So $(u \cdot w)\, v$ cancels $-(w \cdot u)\, v$, and in the same way the terms in $u$ and in $w$ cancel; the sum is the zero vector.

concepts.c:commutative-ring: Commutativity makes the dot product symmetric, so the terms cancel.
concepts.c:cross-product: The identity is about cross products of three vectors.

source.note: The classical proof through the vector triple product expansion (the BAC-CAB rule, mathlib cross_cross_eq_smul_sub_smul).

statement: Every [convex body](c:convex-body) $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ contains a unique [ellipsoid](c:ellipsoid) $E$ of maximal volume, and $K \subseteq c + n(E - c)$, where $c$ is the center of $E$.

hypotheses.text: The set $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge 1$, is a [convex body](c:convex-body): a compact [convex set](c:convex-set) with nonempty interior.

conclusion: The maximal inscribed ellipsoid exists and is unique, and its dilation by the factor $n$ about its center contains $K$.

proofs.name: Compactness, averaging and enlargement
proofs.slogan: Get a maximal ellipsoid by compactness, prove uniqueness by averaging, and show that a point of $K$ beyond distance $n$ would allow a larger ellipsoid.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$. Steps 4 and 5 first move $E$ to the unit ball by an affine map, which keeps ratios of volumes.

roles.why: Compactness bounds the ellipsoids, convexity puts averages and hulls inside $K$, and the interior gives positive volume.

steps.slogan: Maximize the volume over the compact set of ellipsoids inside $K$.
steps.detail: Write an ellipsoid as $AB + c$ with $A$ symmetric positive semidefinite and $B$ the [unit ball](c:unit-ball); its volume is $\det A \cdot |B|$. The pairs $(A, c)$ with $AB + c \subseteq K$ form a closed bounded set and $\det$ is continuous, so a maximizer exists, with $\det A > 0$ because $K$ contains a ball.

steps.slogan: Average two maximal ellipsoids and compare their [determinants](c:determinant).
steps.detail: For maximal $A_1 B + c_1$ and $A_2 B + c_2$, convexity puts $\frac{A_1 + A_2}{2} B + \frac{c_1 + c_2}{2}$ in $K$. With eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $A_1^{-1/2} A_2 A_1^{-1/2}$, whose product is $1$, AM-GM gives $\det \frac{A_1 + A_2}{2} = \det A_1 \prod \frac{1 + \lambda_i}{2} \ge \det A_1$; maximality forces equality, so $A_1 = A_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that two maximal ellipsoids with the same matrix have the same center.
steps.detail: The [affine map](c:affine-map) $y \mapsto A^{-1}(y - c_1)$ turns them into $B$ and $B + d$. If $d \ne 0$, the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $B \cup (B + d)$ contains the ellipsoid with center $d/2$, semi-axis $1 + |d|/2$ along $d$ and $1$ across, which has larger volume. So $d = 0$.

steps.slogan: Build a larger ellipsoid in the hull of the ball and a far point.
steps.detail: Move $E$ to $B$ and suppose that $x \in K$ has $|x| = t > n$, say $x = t e_1$. For small $\varepsilon > 0$, a support-function check shows that the ellipsoid with center $\varepsilon e_1$, semi-axis $1 + \varepsilon$ along $e_1$ and $(1 - 2\varepsilon/(t-1))^{1/2}$ across lies in the convex hull of $B \cup \{x\}$.

steps.slogan: Compare the volumes and conclude that $K$ lies in $nB$.
steps.detail: The volume ratio $(1 + \varepsilon)(1 - 2\varepsilon/(t-1))^{(n-1)/2}$ has derivative $1 - (n-1)/(t-1) > 0$ at $\varepsilon = 0$, so it exceeds $1$ for small $\varepsilon$, against maximality. Hence $K \subseteq nB$, that is $K \subseteq c + n(E - c)$; with steps 2 and 3, $E$ is unique.

concepts.c:convex-body: The theorem is about ellipsoids inscribed in a convex body.
concepts.c:ellipsoid: Ellipsoids are the competitors whose volume is maximized.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity puts averaged ellipsoids and convex hulls inside $K$.
concepts.c:unit-ball: Every ellipsoid is an affine image of the unit ball.
concepts.c:determinant: The volume of $AB + c$ is $\det A$ times the ball volume.
concepts.c:affine-map: Affine maps move the maximal ellipsoid to the unit ball.
concepts.c:convex-hull: Hulls of balls and points contain the larger competing ellipsoids.

source.note: A direct proof by compactness, determinant averaging and an explicit larger ellipsoid; F. John's original 1948 proof uses Lagrange-multiplier conditions instead.
